title: How to Plan Peak Season Fulfillment With a Network Like Gooten
excerpt: Peak season breaks fulfillment plans that worked all summer. This planning guide covers capacity, routing, cutoff dates, and backup decisions for stores running a distributed production network.
body: A fulfillment setup that sailed through summer usually breaks in November, and it rarely breaks all at once. Production slows, carriers miss scans, and the long tail of your catalog turns into a pile of support tickets. Planning for peak season is less about finding a magic partner and more about removing the decisions that cost you days in December. The Fulfillment & Shipping category at /category/fulfillment keeps the current shortlist with ratings and pricing for production and shipping partners.

Start by learning how your network routes orders. A distributed production model picks a facility based on the destination, the item, and current capacity, which is efficient right up until one region saturates. Read the partner documentation and find out where the facilities actually sit and which items are produced in more than one place. The tool overview at /tool/gooten lays out how that routing and catalog model works, and knowing it helps you predict which SKUs are single points of failure before the season begins.

Work backward from the delivery date. Take the last day you can promise arrival, subtract carrier transit time with a realistic holiday buffer, subtract production time, and you have your real internal cutoff. Publish a conservative version of that date on the site and in your checkout messaging. Customers forgive a date they were told in advance far more easily than a package that misses a promise, and every missed promise becomes a support conversation during the busiest weeks of your year.

Cut the catalog before the rush, not during it. Long tail SKUs that sell once a month consume the same operational attention as a hero product when something goes wrong, and in peak season they are usually produced by a single facility with no fallback. Identify the twenty percent of SKUs driving most of your revenue, confirm each one has a viable backup production path, and quietly unpublish the rest until January. A smaller catalog also makes ad spend more efficient, because you are concentrating demand instead of spreading it thin.

Then decide what you will do when something fails anyway. A replacement path matters more than a perfect plan: know which SKUs can be reproduced quickly, which hero items could ship from a second partner, and who answers the customer when a parcel stalls. Draft the macros and the refund policy now, while nobody is angry. Peak season support is mostly volume management, and a prepared response that ships a replacement beats a thoughtful apology that arrives three days after the gifting deadline.

This kind of planning fits stores doing enough volume that a bad December would be visible in the annual numbers, and especially stores selling giftable items with a hard delivery deadline. It matters less if your sales are evenly spread and nothing you sell is time sensitive. Either way, do the routing homework and the cutoff math early, because both get harder once the queue is full.
